scenes.head: Mortgages
scenes.sub: A home loan is an annuity with a house attached. Calculate a fixed-rate mortgage payment, compare 30- and 15-year terms, find the balance after any number of years, decide whether discount points and extra payments pay off, see what inflation does to a fixed payment, and read how an adjustable-rate mortgage resets.

segs.say: Mortgages. A home loan is an annuity with a house attached. Calculate a fixed-rate mortgage payment, compare 30- and 15-year terms, find the balance after any number of years, decide whether discount points and extra payments pay off, see what inflation does to a fixed payment, and read how an adjustable-rate mortgage resets.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate the monthly principal-and-interest payment, the total interest and the balance after k years on a fixed-rate mortgage.
Compare a 30-year and a 15-year mortgage on payment, total interest and how fast the balance falls.
Evaluate discount points by their simple break-even time and by the present value of the savings over the time the loan is kept.
Calculate how much time and interest regular extra payments save, using logarithms to find the new term.
Calculate the real value of a fixed mortgage payment under inflation, and the new payment when an adjustable-rate mortgage resets within its caps.

scenes.head: March 2027.

segs.say: March 2027. Jonah, a secondary-school teacher and an old friend of Ana’s, has agreed to buy a house for $360,000. He will pay $72,000 (20%) from his savings and borrow the other $288,000. His credit union (fictional, as are all the rates in this lesson) offers three fixed-rate loans: 30 years at 6.5%; 30 years at 6.125% if he pays 1.5 discount points upfront; or 15 years at 5.875%. Ana, who hopes to buy a flat of her own one day, is watching closely: the course project asks you to make the same kind of choice for her, with her own numbers.

chapters.title: A mortgage is an amortising loan

scenes.head: A mortgage is a loan to buy a property, secured on that property: if the borrower does not repay as agreed, the lender can take it.

segs.say: A mortgage is a loan to buy a property, secured on that property: if the borrower does not repay as agreed, the lender can take it. With a fixed-rate mortgage the interest rate never changes, so the borrower pays the same amount every month for the whole term. Each payment covers the interest due for the month and repays some principal, so the balance falls to zero by the last payment: the loan is repaid by amortisation, exactly as in the loan-amortisation lesson. The only differences are scale and length: hundreds of thousands of dollars over 180 or 360 months.

scenes.head: The rate is quoted per year and charged monthly, so the monthly rate is the annual rate ÷ 12.

segs.say: The rate is quoted per year and charged monthly, so the monthly rate is the annual rate ÷ 12. For Jonah’s 30-year offer, r = 0.065 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.00541667 and n = 360 payments. The payment is the level annuity whose present value at r equals the loan:

scenes.head: In the first month the interest is 288,000 × 0.065 ÷ 12 = 1,560.00 dollars, so only $260.36 of the $1,820.36 repays principal.

segs.say: In the first month the interest is 288,000 × 0.065 ÷ 12 = 1,560.00 dollars, so only $260.36 of the $1,820.36 repays principal. Interest is charged on the balance, the balance starts large, and so early payments are mostly interest. As the balance shrinks, the interest part shrinks and the principal part grows; by the last payment it is almost all principal. Over 30 years Jonah would pay about $655,328.13 in total, of which about $367,328.13 is interest: more than the $288,000 he borrows.

scenes.head: Principal and interest are not the whole monthly bill

segs.say: Principal and interest are not the whole monthly bill. The formula gives the payment of principal and interest only. Many lenders also collect property taxes and homeowners insurance through an escrow account funded from each monthly payment, and the CFPB notes that because taxes and premiums change from year to year, the escrow part, and so the total payment, changes too. If Jonah’s taxes and insurance come to a fictional $540 a month, his total monthly payment would be about $2,360.36 at first, and only the $1,820.36 is fixed for 30 years.

scenes.head: A shorter term means larger payments but far less interest, because the balance is paid down faster and there are fewer months on which to charge…

segs.say: A shorter term means larger payments but far less interest, because the balance is paid down faster and there are fewer months on which to charge interest. Jonah’s credit union also charges a lower rate for the shorter term.
Jonah’s two no-points offers on $288,000 (fictional rates)

scenes.head: The 15-year loan costs $590.55 a month more but saves about $221,365.90 of interest, and after five years Jonah would owe about $51,209 less.

segs.say: The 15-year loan costs $590.55 a month more but saves about $221,365.90 of interest, and after five years Jonah would owe about $51,209 less. Total interest overstates the saving, though: much of that gap is the result of repaying the loan in half the time, and each loan’s payments are worth exactly $288,000 at its own rate. The real gain is the lower rate, which is worth far less than the interest gap suggests. The 30-year loan’s advantage is flexibility: a lower required payment leaves room in the budget, and, as the theory section shows, he can still choose to pay it off faster.

chapters.title: Buying a lower rate: discount points

scenes.head: Discount points are an upfront fee paid at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate.

segs.say: Discount points are an upfront fee paid at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explains that one point costs 1% of the loan amount and that how much a point lowers the rate varies by lender, loan type and market conditions. Jonah’s 1.5 points would cost 0.015 × 288,000 = 4,320 dollars and cut his rate from 6.5% to 6.125%, which lowers the payment to about $1,749.92, a saving of about $70.44 a month.

scenes.head: The simple break-even time divides the cost by the monthly saving: 4,320 ÷ 70.44 ≈ 61.3 months, a little over five years.

segs.say: The simple break-even time divides the cost by the monthly saving: 4,320 ÷ 70.44 ≈ 61.3 months, a little over five years. If Jonah sells or refinances before then, the points lose him money; if he keeps the loan longer, they pay off. The opposite trade also exists: a lender credit lowers closing costs in exchange for a higher rate, which suits a borrower who expects to move or refinance soon.

scenes.head: Every mortgage decision is a time-value decision

segs.say: Every mortgage decision is a time-value decision. Points trade cash today for smaller payments later; a shorter term trades higher payments now for less interest later; extra payments trade spending now for a shorter loan. Each is judged by comparing the present value of what you give up with the present value of what you save, over the time you actually expect to keep the loan.

chapters.title: The payment formula and the schedule

scenes.head: With loan PV, monthly rate r and n monthly payments, the payment is C = PV × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ]: the annuity formula of module 3 solved for the…

segs.say: With loan PV, monthly rate r and n monthly payments, the payment is C = PV × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ]: the annuity formula of module 3 solved for the payment. Each month the interest is the opening balance times r, the principal repaid is C minus that interest, and the new balance is the old balance minus the principal repaid. The first three months of Jonah’s 30-year schedule:
The start of Jonah’s 30-year schedule ($288,000 at 6.5%, payment $1,820.36)

scenes.head: The principal repaid grows by the factor 1 + r each month, so the balance falls slowly at first and quickly at the end.

segs.say: The principal repaid grows by the factor 1 + r each month, so the balance falls slowly at first and quickly at the end. Jonah would have repaid only 6.4% of the loan after five years and 15.2% after ten; the halfway point comes in month 257, about 21 years in. The chart in “Explore” shows each year’s payments split into interest and principal.

scenes.head: The loan-amortisation lesson gave two equivalent methods.

segs.say: The loan-amortisation lesson gave two equivalent methods. Prospectively, the balance after k payments is the present value of the payments still to come: Bₖ = C × [1 − (1 + r)^(−(n − k))] ÷ r. Retrospectively, it is what the loan would have grown to, less what the payments made would have grown to. After ten years Jonah’s 30-year balance is 1,820.36 × [1 − 1.00541667⁻²⁴⁰] ÷ 0.00541667 ≈ 244,155.24 dollars. This is the figure a buyer needs when planning to sell or refinance: the sale must repay it.

scenes.head: The simple break-even (cost ÷ monthly saving) ignores two things that pull in opposite directions.

segs.say: The simple break-even (cost ÷ monthly saving) ignores two things that pull in opposite directions. The lower rate also pays the balance down a little faster, so a seller owes slightly less; and a dollar of saving in year five is worth less than a dollar of points paid today. A sounder test values every cash flow of the points loan at the rate Jonah would otherwise pay, 6.5%. The no-points loan is worth exactly $288,000 at 6.5% for any holding period, by construction. The points loan, kept k months and then repaid, costs:

scenes.head: If that is less than $288,000, the points were worth buying.

segs.say: If that is less than $288,000, the points were worth buying. Valuing at 6.5% treats the alternative to paying points as borrowing the $4,320 at the loan rate, or using it to prepay the loan. If the cash would otherwise earn less in savings, discounting at that lower rate makes the points look better; the rate is a judgement, so state it. For Jonah it is about $614.50 more than $288,000 if he keeps the loan four years, and about $3,107.38 less if he keeps it ten. The crossover comes at about 58 months, close to the simple estimate here because the two omitted effects nearly cancel. With higher rates or a larger rate cut, they need not.

scenes.head: Points and the APR in US mortgage disclosures (CFPB)

segs.say: Points and the APR in US mortgage disclosures (CFPB). For a mortgage, the APR that lenders disclose under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) is broader than the interest rate: the CFPB explains that it reflects the interest rate, any points, mortgage broker fees and other charges paid to get the loan, so it is usually higher than the rate. Regulation Z lists points and loan fees among the components of the finance charge (12 CFR §1026.4(b)(3)). On a Loan Estimate the interest rate appears on page 1, points on page 2 (section A) and the APR on page 3. For an adjustable-rate loan, the CFPB warns, the APR does not reflect the maximum rate the loan could reach.

scenes.head: Treating the $4,320 of points as the only finance charge, the APR of Jonah’s points loan is the rate at which 360 payments of $1,749.92 are worth…

segs.say: Treating the $4,320 of points as the only finance charge, the APR of Jonah’s points loan is the rate at which 360 payments of $1,749.92 are worth what he actually receives, 288,000 − 4,320 = 283,680 dollars. By trial, or with a spreadsheet’s RATE function, that is about 6.27%, against 6.5% for the no-points loan. The APR spreads the points over the full 30 years, so it flatters points for anyone who will not keep the loan that long: kept for four years, the same loan costs about 6.56% a year. Compare APRs between loans of the same type and term, and then ask how long you will really keep the loan.

scenes.head: Prepayment, paying principal ahead of schedule, saves interest because every extra dollar stops being charged interest from that month onward.

segs.say: Prepayment, paying principal ahead of schedule, saves interest because every extra dollar stops being charged interest from that month onward. If the borrower keeps paying a fixed larger amount C, the number of months needed solves PV = C × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r for n, using logarithms as in the annuities lesson:

Adding $250 a month to Jonah’s 30-year payment, so C = 2,070.36: r × PV ÷ C = 1,560 ÷ 2,070.36 ≈ 0.753494, and n = −ln (0.246506) ÷ ln (1.00541667) ≈ 1.400367 ÷ 0.005402 ≈ 259.23. He would make 259 full payments and a smaller 260th, finishing in 21 years 8 months instead of 30 years. Running the schedule shows total interest of about $248,697.14, a saving of about $118,630.99.

scenes.head: Before planning extra payments, check the loan for a prepayment penalty.

segs.say: Before planning extra payments, check the loan for a prepayment penalty. The CFPB explains that not all mortgages have one; where a loan does, it typically applies when the whole balance is paid off within a set period, usually three or five years, for example by selling or refinancing, and small extra principal payments normally do not trigger it.

chapters.title: A fixed payment in an inflating world

scenes.head: A fixed-rate mortgage payment is a fixed nominal amount: $1,820.36 in 2027 and $1,820.36 in 2056.

segs.say: A fixed-rate mortgage payment is a fixed nominal amount: $1,820.36 in 2027 and $1,820.36 in 2056. With inflation, later payments are made in dollars that buy less. Measured in today’s dollars with the method of the previous lesson, the payment made at the end of year t is worth C ÷ (1 + i)ᵗ. At 3% inflation (an assumption for illustration):
Jonah’s $1,820.36 payment in today’s dollars at 3% inflation

scenes.head: The real burden falls further if pay rises with prices.

segs.say: The real burden falls further if pay rises with prices. On a fictional salary of $92,000 a year, $1,820.36 is about 23.7% of Jonah’s gross monthly pay at the start; if his pay rises 3% a year, it is about 17.7% ten years later. In real terms the loan costs less than its quoted rate: the 6.5% compounded monthly is an effective annual rate of about 6.697%, a real interest rate of about 1.06697 ÷ 1.03 − 1 ≈ 3.59% at 3% inflation. With a fixed rate, the lender bears the risk that inflation turns out higher than expected; the borrower bears the risk that it turns out lower.

scenes.head: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) moves the interest-rate risk the other way.

segs.say: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) moves the interest-rate risk the other way. Its rate is fixed for an initial period (five years in worked example 4) and then resets at regular intervals. The CFPB explains the reset: the new rate is an index, an interest rate that moves with market conditions and that the lender chooses when you apply, plus a margin, a number of percentage points set in the loan agreement that does not change after closing. Index plus margin is called the fully indexed rate, and the actual new rate is that figure subject to the loan’s rate caps.
Initial adjustment cap: how far the rate can move at the first reset; the CFPB says two or five percentage points is common.
Subsequent adjustment cap: how far it can move at each later reset; most commonly one or two points.
Lifetime cap: how far it can move in total over the life of the loan; most commonly five points.

scenes.head: At each reset the payment is recalculated with the payment formula: the current balance, the new monthly rate and the months remaining.

segs.say: At each reset the payment is recalculated with the payment formula: the current balance, the new monthly rate and the months remaining. Worked example 4 shows the jump a borrower can face at the first reset, and why the right question about an ARM is not “what is the starting payment?” but “what is the highest payment the caps allow, and could I afford it?”

scenes.head: Fixed-rate mortgage payment (principal and interest)

segs.say: Fixed-rate mortgage payment (principal and interest): C = PV × r/(1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ), r = (annual rate)/12, n = 12t.
C: Monthly payment of principal and interest ($ per month).
PV: Amount borrowed: the price less the down payment ($).
r: Monthly interest rate: the annual interest rate in the loan contract ÷ 12, as a decimal (not the disclosed APR, which also includes points and fees) (per month).
n: Number of monthly payments (months).
t: Term of the loan (years).
It assumes this: Payments at the end of each month; the rate is fixed for the whole term.
Property taxes, homeowners insurance and any escrow payments are extra.

scenes.head: Mortgage balance after k monthly payments

segs.say: Mortgage balance after k monthly payments: Bₖ = C × (1 − (1 + r)^(−(n − k)))/r.
Bₖ: Balance still owed immediately after payment k ($).
C: Monthly payment ($ per month).
r: Monthly interest rate (per month).
n: Total number of payments in the term (months).
k: Number of payments already made (months).
The prospective balance card from the loan-amortisation lesson, with monthly periods; its retrospective card gives the same figure.

scenes.head: Discount points: cost and simple break-even

segs.say: Discount points: cost and simple break-even: Cost of points = p × 1% × PV, Break-even ≈ (Cost of points)/(C₀ − C₁).
p: Number of points bought (may be fractional) (points).
PV: Loan amount ($).
C₀: Monthly payment without points ($ per month).
C₁: Monthly payment at the lower rate ($ per month).
Break-even: Months of saving needed to recover the cost, ignoring time value (months).
It assumes this: Ignores the faster fall in the balance and the time value of money; the present-value test in “In depth” includes both.
How much one point lowers the rate varies by lender, loan type and market conditions.

scenes.head: APR with points (points as the only finance charge)

segs.say: APR with points (points as the only finance charge): PV − F = C × (1 − (1 + q)⁻ⁿ)/q, APR = 12 × q.
PV: Loan amount ($).
F: Fees paid up front: here the cost of the points, paid at closing ($).
C: Monthly payment at the contract rate ($ per month).
q: Monthly rate that solves the equation, found by trial or a spreadsheet RATE function (per month).
n: Number of monthly payments (months).
APR: Annual percentage rate including the points (per year).
It assumes this: Points are the only finance charge beyond interest and the loan runs its full term.

The loan-amortisation lesson’s APR-with-fee card with m = 12, writing q for the solving rate to keep it apart from the contract rate r. A disclosed APR also includes broker fees and other finance charges, calculated under Regulation Z.

scenes.head: Months to repay with a larger payment

segs.say: Months to repay with a larger payment: n = −(ln (1 − (r × PV)/C))/(ln (1 + r)).
n: Months needed to repay the balance (round up: the last payment is smaller) (months).
r: Monthly interest rate (per month).
PV: Balance to be repaid ($).
C: Monthly payment, including the extra amount ($ per month).
It assumes this: The larger payment is kept up every month; no prepayment penalty applies.
Only defined when C exceeds r × PV, the first month’s interest.

scenes.head: Real value of a fixed payment

segs.say: Real value of a fixed payment: Real value in year t = C/(1 + i)ᵗ.
C: Fixed nominal payment ($).
i: Annual inflation rate (per year).
t: Years from today (years).
From the previous lesson: a fixed nominal amount loses purchasing power at the inflation rate.

scenes.head: Adjustable-rate mortgage: the new rate

segs.say: Adjustable-rate mortgage: the new rate: Fully indexed rate = Index + Margin; new rate within current rate ± adjustment cap and initial rate ± lifetime cap.
Fully indexed rate: Index plus margin: the rate before any caps apply (% per year).
Index: A market interest rate named in the loan, which changes over time (% per year).
Margin: Percentage points added to the index, fixed in the loan agreement (percentage points).
adjustment cap: Most the rate can move at one reset (the initial cap at the first reset, the subsequent cap after) (percentage points).
lifetime cap: Most the rate can move over the life of the loan (percentage points).
current rate: The rate charged before this reset (% per year).
initial rate: The loan’s starting rate (% per year).
After each reset, recalculate C from the current balance, the new monthly rate and the months remaining. Some loans also set a floor (CFPB).

scenes.head: Jonah’s 30-year payment

segs.say: Jonah borrows $288,000 for 30 years at a fixed 6.5% a year, repaid monthly. Find the monthly payment of principal and interest, how the first payment splits, and the total interest over the term.

scenes.head: Jonah’s 30-year payment

segs.say: Step 1. Monthly rate and number of payments: r = 0.065 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.00541667; n = 12 × 30 = 360.
Step 2. Discount factor and annuity factor: 1.00541667⁻³⁶⁰ ≈ 0.143025, so [1 − 0.143025] ÷ 0.00541667 ≈ 158.2108.
Step 5. Total interest: 360 × 1,820.3559 − 288,000 ≈ 367,328.13 dollars (using the unrounded payment).

scenes.head: Jonah’s 30-year payment

segs.say: A payment of about $1,820.36 a month; the first payment is $1,560.00 of interest and $260.36 of principal; total interest about $367,328.13.

Jonah would pay back about 2.28 times what he borrows. The early payments barely dent the balance, which is why the balance after a few years, not the original loan, is what matters if he sells or refinances.

scenes.head: Are 1.5 points worth $4,320?

segs.say: Jonah can cut his 30-year rate from 6.5% to 6.125% by paying 1.5 points on $288,000. Find the cost, the monthly saving and the simple break-even, then test the decision properly for a four-year and a ten-year stay by valuing the points loan’s cash flows at 6.5%.

scenes.head: Are 1.5 points worth $4,320?

segs.say: Step 1. Cost: 1.5 × 1% × 288,000 = 4,320 dollars. New payment at 0.06125 ÷ 12 over 360 months: about $1,749.92, against $1,820.36. Saving about $70.44 a month.
Step 2. Simple break-even: 4,320 ÷ 70.44 ≈ 61.3 months, about 5 years 1 month.

Step 3. Four-year stay. Balance on the points loan after 48 payments: about $272,818.58. At r = 0.065 ÷ 12, the 48-month annuity factor is about 42.167488 and the discount factor 1.00541667⁻⁴⁸ ≈ 0.77159277. Value of the points loan, with the unrounded payment of $1,749.9184: 4,320 + 1,749.9184 × 42.167488 + 272,818.58 × 0.77159277 ≈ 288,614.50 (calculated with unrounded figures), which is $614.50 more than the $288,000 the no-points loan is worth.

Step 4. Ten-year stay. Balance after 120 payments about $241,814.64; annuity factor about 88.0685; discount factor about 0.52296229. Value: 4,320 + 1,749.9184 × 88.0685 + 241,814.64 × 0.52296229 ≈ 284,892.62 (unrounded figures), about $3,107.38 less than $288,000.
Step 5. Crossover: repeating the test month by month, the points start to pay off from about month 58.

scenes.head: Are 1.5 points worth $4,320?

segs.say: The points cost $4,320 and save about $70.44 a month: a simple break-even of about 61 months. In present-value terms they lose about $614.50 if Jonah keeps the loan four years and gain about $3,107.38 if he keeps it ten; the crossover is about 58 months.

Points are a bet on staying put. Jonah should buy them only if he is fairly confident of keeping this loan for well over five years, with no sale or refinancing in between. If rates might fall, so that refinancing becomes attractive, the case for points weakens.

chapters.title: Example: A 15-year loan, or a 30-year loan paid faster?

scenes.head: A 15-year loan, or a 30-year loan paid faster?

segs.say: Jonah earns a fictional $92,000 a year. He likes the idea of being debt-free sooner but worries about committing to $2,410.90 a month. Compare (a) the 15-year loan at 5.875%, (b) the 30-year loan at 6.5% with $250 a month extra, and (c) the 30-year loan paid at the 15-year payment of $2,410.90 by choice.

scenes.head: A 15-year loan, or a 30-year loan paid faster?

segs.say: Step 1. Required payments as a share of gross monthly pay ($92,000 ÷ 12 ≈ $7,666.67): 15-year $2,410.90, about 31.4%; 30-year $1,820.36, about 23.7%.

Step 2. (b) With $250 extra, C = 2,070.36. Months: n = −ln (1 − 1,560 ÷ 2,070.36) ÷ ln (1.00541667) ≈ 259.23, so 260 payments, about 21 years 8 months. Total interest by the schedule about $248,697.14, saving about $118,630.99 against the scheduled 30 years.
Step 3. Paying $2,410.90 a month on the 30-year loan clears it in 193 months with total interest of about $176,798.18, against about $145,962.23 on the 15-year loan.

Step 4. The difference, about $30,835.95, is what the 15-year loan’s lower rate is worth if Jonah would really pay that much every month; it is the price of keeping the right to pay less in a bad month.

scenes.head: A 15-year loan, or a 30-year loan paid faster?

segs.say: The 15-year loan is cheapest (interest about $145,962.23) if Jonah can always pay $2,410.90. Paying the 30-year loan at the same amount costs about $30,835.95 more in interest but keeps a required payment of only $1,820.36; $250 extra a month clears it in about 21 years 8 months and saves about $118,630.99.

Commitment is cheaper; flexibility has a price. A borrower with a secure income and a full emergency fund should lean to the 15-year loan; one whose income may dip, or who wants to keep cash for other goals, may rationally pay more interest for the 30-year loan and prepay when he can, after checking that the loan has no prepayment penalty.

scenes.head: An adjustable-rate mortgage resets

segs.say: Instead, Jonah is offered a fictional ARM on $288,000: 5.75% fixed for five years, then resetting once a year to an index plus a 2.75-point margin, amortised over 30 years. Caps: 2 points at the first reset, 1 point at each later reset, 5 points over the life of the loan. At the first reset the index is 4.5%. Find the payment before and after the reset, and the most the rate could ever reach.

scenes.head: An adjustable-rate mortgage resets

segs.say: Step 1. Starting payment at 0.0575 ÷ 12 over 360 months: about $1,680.69, which is $139.67 less than the fixed 6.5% loan.
Step 2. Balance after 60 payments (prospective method at the starting rate): 1,680.69 × [1 − 1.00479167⁻³⁰⁰] ÷ 0.00479167 ≈ 267,155.10.
Step 3. New rate: fully indexed 4.5% + 2.75% = 7.25%; the first-reset cap allows up to 5.75% + 2% = 7.75%, so the rate becomes 7.25%.
Step 4. New payment: $267,155.10 over the remaining 300 months at 0.0725 ÷ 12 gives about $1,931.02, a rise of about $250.33 (14.9%).

Step 5. Worst cases: had the index been above 5.0%, the cap would have held the rate at 7.75% and the payment at about $2,017.90. Over the life of the loan the rate can never exceed 5.75% + 5% = 10.75%.

scenes.head: An adjustable-rate mortgage resets

segs.say: About $1,680.69 a month for five years, then about $1,931.02 at 7.25%; the cap limits the first reset to 7.75% (about $2,017.90), and the rate can never exceed 10.75%.

The ARM was cheaper for five years and dearer afterwards in this scenario. It suits a borrower who expects to sell or refinance before the first reset, or who could absorb the capped worst-case payment; it does not suit one who chose it only because the starting payment was lower.

scenes.head: Fixed-rate mortgage explorer

segs.say: Start with Jonah’s loan. Shorten the term, change the rate, add an extra monthly payment and watch the balance line fall faster; the rows show the months and interest saved and what the final scheduled payment is worth after inflation. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Are the points worth it?

segs.say: Points against holding period. Change the number of points, how much each one cuts the rate, and how long you keep the loan. Compare the simple break-even with the present-value test, and find the holding period at which buying points stops making sense. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Where Jonah’s payments go each year ($288,000 at 6.5% over 30 years)

segs.say: Each year’s twelve payments on Jonah’s 30-year loan, split into interest and principal. The total is the same every year; only the split changes. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Using the annual rate with monthly payments

segs.say: Using the annual rate with monthly payments. The payment uses the monthly rate (annual ÷ 12) and the number of months (12 × years). Using 6.5% with 360 periods gives about $18,720 a month, which is absurd; working out an annual payment over 30 years and dividing by 12 gives about $1,837.86, which looks plausible but is still wrong, because interest is charged monthly.

scenes.head: Treating the payment as the whole housing cost

segs.say: Treating the payment as the whole housing cost. The formula covers principal and interest only. Property taxes and homeowners insurance, often collected through escrow, come on top and can change every year.

scenes.head: Judging points by the APR alone

segs.say: Judging points by the APR alone. The APR spreads points over the full term. If you will sell or refinance in a few years, the cost of the loan over the time you actually keep it can be higher than the no-points loan, even though its APR is lower.

scenes.head: Thinking the balance falls evenly

segs.say: Thinking the balance falls evenly. After a third of the term, Jonah would have repaid less than a sixth of the loan. Interest dominates early payments; find the balance with the balance formula, not by subtracting payments.

scenes.head: Comparing an ARM’s starting payment with a fixed payment

segs.say: Comparing an ARM’s starting payment with a fixed payment. The starting payment lasts only for the fixed period. Compare the fixed payment with the payment the caps allow after resets, and plan for the worst case.

scenes.head: Forgetting inflation when judging a 30-year commitment

segs.say: Forgetting inflation when judging a 30-year commitment. A fixed payment of $1,820.36 is worth about $750 in today’s dollars by year 30 at 3% inflation. The real burden falls over time, though only inflation that turns out higher than expected helps the borrower beyond what the rate already allowed for.

scenes.head: Jonah takes the 30-year fixed loan without points.

segs.say: Jonah takes the 30-year fixed loan without points. He expects to stay in the house for many years, but his school may relocate him within five, and the simple and present-value break-evens both say he would need to stay about five years for points to pay. He sets up an automatic extra $250 a month, after confirming with the credit union that the loan has no prepayment penalty, and keeps the option to stop if his budget tightens. Ana notes the method: in the project you will run the same comparison for her, with her own loan, rates and points offer.

scenes.head: Comparing Loan Estimates.

segs.say: Comparing Loan Estimates. A loan officer at a fictional credit union helps a nurse compare three quotes received the same week for the same loan type and term. She lines up the interest rates on page 1, the points and fees on page 2 and the APRs on page 3, then asks the question the APR cannot answer: how long will you keep this loan? For a buyer likely to move within four years she points out the no-points or lender-credit options; for one planning to stay fifteen years, the points option.

scenes.head: Preparing for an ARM reset.

segs.say: Preparing for an ARM reset. A housing counsellor meets a fictional couple whose five-year ARM resets in six months. She finds their current balance, the index level and the margin from their loan documents, computes the payment at the fully indexed rate and at the cap, and compares both with their budget. If the capped payment would strain them, she sets out the alternatives early: refinancing to a fixed rate, making extra payments now to reduce the balance, or adjusting the budget.

scenes.head: A business buying its premises.

segs.say: A business buying its premises. The owner of a fictional dental practice compares renting with buying a small building financed by a commercial mortgage. The same arithmetic applies: the payment formula, the balance after the years she expects to stay, and the present value of the costs of each option at her required return. Because the mortgage payment is fixed while her rent would rise with an escalation clause, she makes the comparison in real terms, as in the previous lesson.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A fixed-rate mortgage is an amortising loan: C = PV × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)^−n] with r = annual rate ÷ 12 and n = months. Taxes, insurance and escrow are extra.
Early payments are mostly interest; the balance after k payments is the present value of the remaining payments.
A 15-year loan has higher payments and far less total interest than a 30-year loan; a 30-year loan with voluntary extra payments buys flexibility at a price.
One discount point costs 1% of the loan. Simple break-even = cost ÷ monthly saving; the sounder test values the points loan’s cash flows over the expected holding period.
The disclosed mortgage APR includes points and other finance charges but assumes the loan runs its full term.
Extra payments shorten the term: n = −ln(1 − rPV ÷ C) ÷ ln(1 + r). Check for a prepayment penalty first.
Inflation reduces the real value of a fixed payment: C ÷ (1 + i)^t.
An ARM resets to index + margin within initial, subsequent and lifetime caps; judge it by the capped worst-case payment.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
